summary: This chapter covers the main types of government and the ideas that shaped American democracy. GED questions often give you a short passage, such as a line from the Declaration of Independence, and ask which principle it shows.

Governments differ in who holds power. In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws themselves. In a representative democracy, or republic, citizens elect officials to make laws. A monarchy is led by a king or queen who usually inherits the job, and a totalitarian government controls almost every part of life. In a parliamentary system the prime minister comes from the legislature, while in a presidential system the president is elected separately.

American democracy rests on a few key principles. Natural rights are rights people are born with, such as life and liberty. Consent of the governed means government gets its power from the people. Rule of law means no one is above the law. Majority rule is balanced by minority rights, and a written constitution limits what government may do.

concepts.definition: Direct democracy: citizens vote on laws. Representative democracy (republic): citizens elect officials who make laws.
Rights every person has from birth, such as life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Government cannot rightly take them away.
concepts.tip: Look for "unalienable rights" or "endowed by their Creator."

concepts.definition: Government gets its fair power from the people it governs. Also called popular sovereignty.
concepts.tip: "We the People" = the people are the source of power.

concepts.definition: Laws apply to everyone equally, including leaders. No one is above the law.
concepts.tip: A leader punished for breaking the law shows rule of law.

concepts.definition: The majority decides, but it cannot take away the basic rights of smaller groups.
concepts.tip: A vote cannot cancel protected rights such as freedom of religion.

concepts.definition: Power is divided between the national government and the state governments.
concepts.tip: Federalism = levels; separation of powers = branches.

concepts.definition: A government with total control: one party, controlled media, secret police, and no real limits.
concepts.tip: One party plus control of private life = totalitarian.

points: Know which principle a famous quote shows: natural rights, consent of the governed, or limited government.
Federalist No. 51 argues that government must control the people and also control itself.
Do not mix up federalism (national vs. state) with separation of powers (three branches).
The Constitution creates no hereditary offices.

compare.title: Types of government
rows: One party or ruler with total control

summary: This chapter explains how the U.S. government is built. The Constitution splits power among three branches and between the national and state governments, so no single group can hold all power. This is the biggest topic on the test, because civics and government is about half of it.

Congress, the legislative branch, makes laws. It has two parts: the Senate, with two senators from each state serving 6-year terms, and the House of Representatives, with seats based on population and 2-year terms. The President leads the executive branch and carries out laws for 4-year terms. The courts, led by the Supreme Court, form the judicial branch and interpret laws.

Each branch can check the others. The President can veto bills, and Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers. The Senate confirms judges and Cabinet members. Courts can strike down unconstitutional laws (judicial review). The House impeaches officials and the Senate holds the trial.

Some powers belong only to the federal government, such as printing money and declaring war. Others belong to the states, such as issuing driver's licenses. Some, such as taxing, are shared. Amending the Constitution usually takes a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states.

concepts.definition: Legislative (Congress) makes laws; executive (President) carries them out; judicial (courts) interprets them.
The President can veto a bill. Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
Courts can strike down laws or actions that break the Constitution. Established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
concepts.tip: Court rules a law unconstitutional = judicial check.

concepts.definition: The House votes to impeach (charge) an official. The Senate holds the trial; two-thirds of senators present are needed to convict.
Usually two-thirds of both houses of Congress propose, and three-fourths of the states ratify.
Federal only: money, war, treaties. State: licenses, schools, local police. Shared: taxes, borrowing, courts.
concepts.tip: Shared powers are also called concurrent powers.

points: Senate: 2 per state, 6-year terms. House: based on population, 2-year terms. President: 4-year terms.
The Speaker of the House leads the House; the Vice President is President of the Senate.
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not given to the federal government to the states or the people.
The President nominates judges and Cabinet members; the Senate confirms them.

compare.title: Checks and balances
rows: Override vetoes, confirm appointments, impeach, approve budgets

summary: This chapter covers the rights protected by the Constitution, mainly the Bill of Rights, and the duties of citizens. GED questions often describe a situation and ask which amendment applies.

The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, added in 1791. The First Amendment protects religion, speech, the press, assembly, and petition. The Second protects the right to keep and bear arms. The Fourth bans unreasonable searches and seizures. The Fifth protects against self-incrimination and double jeopardy and guarantees due process. The Sixth promises a speedy, public trial and a lawyer, and the Eighth bans excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishment.

Rights are strong but not unlimited. For example, true threats are not protected speech. Supreme Court cases have applied these rights to new situations: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected students' symbolic speech, and Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires police to warn suspects of their rights. Citizens also have responsibilities, such as obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on juries, and voting.

concepts.definition: Protects freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. Bars an official national religion.
concepts.tip: Five freedoms: RAPPS (religion, assembly, press, petition, speech).

concepts.definition: Protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. Police usually need a warrant.
No one must testify against themselves; no double jeopardy; due process of law.
Right to a speedy and public trial, an impartial jury, and a lawyer in criminal cases.
Bans excessive bail and fines and cruel and unusual punishment.
Everyone must obey laws and pay taxes. Only citizens serve on federal juries and vote in federal elections.
concepts.tip: Jury duty and federal voting are for citizens.

points: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments (1791).
The right to vote at 18 is the 26th Amendment, not part of the Bill of Rights.
Tinker: students keep free speech at school unless it seriously disrupts.
Miranda warnings rest mainly on the Fifth Amendment.

summary: This chapter covers how Americans choose their leaders and try to influence government: political parties, interest groups, campaigns, and elections.

The Democratic and Republican parties are the two major parties; smaller parties are called third parties. Interest groups, such as unions or business groups, try to influence policy by lobbying and supporting candidates. Primary elections choose each party's candidate, and the general election chooses the winner.

The President is chosen through the Electoral College. Each state gets electoral votes equal to its senators plus representatives, and Washington, D.C. gets 3, for a total of 538. A candidate needs 270 to win. Amendments have widened voting rights over time, and campaign messages often use loaded language that you should learn to spot.

concepts.definition: An election in which voters choose a party's candidate for the general election.
The system that chooses the President. A candidate needs 270 of 538 electoral votes.
A private group that tries to influence government on its issues, often by lobbying.
concepts.tip: Parties run candidates; interest groups push issues.

concepts.definition: 15th: no denial because of race. 19th: women. 24th: no poll taxes in federal elections. 26th: age 18.
Words with strong emotion, such as "reckless" or "fool," used to persuade without evidence.
concepts.tip: Emotional words are a sign of bias.

points: Presidential requirements: at least 35, natural-born citizen, 14 years' U.S. residence.
Turnout tables: compare like with like, such as presidential years vs. midterm years.
If no candidate wins 270 electoral votes, the House chooses the President.

summary: This chapter is about public policy, the actions government takes to deal with public issues, and about how to judge arguments and evidence on those issues.

Different levels of government handle different issues. Local governments run services such as trash pickup and local police, while states and the federal government handle wider issues. Policies include laws, regulations, spending, and programs. Regulations, such as limits on pollution, can protect health but also add costs.

GED questions often ask you to evaluate statements about a policy. A fact can be checked; an opinion is a judgment. Good evidence for a policy's success compares results before and after, with other conditions similar. When two things rise together, that is a correlation, which does not prove that one causes the other.

concepts.definition: A plan or course of action government takes to deal with an issue, such as a law, regulation, or program.
concepts.tip: Policy = what government decides to do.

concepts.definition: A government rule that limits or guides what people or businesses do.
A fact can be proven true or false. An opinion is a belief or judgment.
concepts.tip: Words like best, fairest, should signal opinion.

concepts.definition: Two things changing together (correlation) does not prove one causes the other.
concepts.tip: Look for a hidden third factor.

concepts.definition: Strong evidence measures the policy's goal before and after the change, with other conditions similar.
concepts.tip: Speeches and polls are not proof a policy worked.

points: Pick the statement that uses judgment words when asked for an opinion.
Different points of view often weigh the same costs and benefits differently.
Local governments handle many everyday services.

summary: This chapter covers the key documents and events behind American government, from the Magna Carta to the early years of the republic. GED questions often quote these documents and ask about their purpose or main idea.

The Magna Carta (1215) set the idea that even the king must follow the law. The Mayflower Compact (1620) was an early agreement to self-government. The Declaration of Independence (1776), written mainly by Thomas Jefferson, stated natural rights and listed complaints against the king to justify independence.

The first national government, under the Articles of Confederation, was weak: Congress could not tax directly. That led to the Constitution in 1787 and the Bill of Rights in 1791. George Washington became the first President and warned against permanent foreign alliances in his Farewell Address (1796). In 1803, the Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the nation's size.

concepts.definition: An English charter that limited the king's power and protected certain rights.
concepts.tip: Even the king is under the law.

concepts.definition: Pilgrims agreed to form a government and obey laws made for the good of the colony.
Announced independence, stated natural rights and consent of the governed, and listed grievances against the king.
concepts.tip: Grievances = the evidence for breaking away.

concepts.definition: The first U.S. plan of government. Congress was weak and could not tax directly.
concepts.tip: Weak central government led to the Constitution.

concepts.definition: Jefferson bought a huge area west of the Mississippi River from France, roughly doubling the nation's size.

points: Constitution: 1787. Bill of Rights: 1791.
Washington's Farewell Address advised against permanent alliances.
When a question quotes a document, look for its purpose and main idea.

summary: This chapter covers European settlement of the Americas and the westward growth of the United States, including its effects on American Indians.

After 1492, the Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, people, and diseases between the Americas and Europe and Africa. Diseases such as smallpox caused a steep drop in the Native population, because Native peoples had no immunity.

In the 1800s, many Americans believed in Manifest Destiny, the idea that the nation should spread across the continent. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to the forced removal of Native nations and the Trail of Tears. The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of western land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.

concepts.definition: The movement of crops, animals, people, and diseases between the Americas and Europe and Africa after 1492.
concepts.tip: Corn and potatoes to Europe; horses and smallpox to the Americas.

concepts.definition: The 1840s belief that the U.S. was meant to expand across North America.
Led to the forced removal of Native nations from the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi River.
concepts.tip: Led to the Trail of Tears.

concepts.definition: Offered 160 acres of western land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.

points: Disease was the largest single cause of the Native population decline.
Expansion brought land to settlers but cost American Indians their homelands.

summary: This chapter follows the long struggle over slavery and equal rights, from the Civil War to the Civil Rights Movement.

Sectionalism, or loyalty to the North or South over the nation, grew in the 1800s, mostly over slavery, and helped cause the Civil War (1861-1865). After the war, three amendments changed the Constitution: the 13th ended slavery, the 14th made people born in the U.S. citizens and promised equal protection, and the 15th barred denying the vote because of race.

After Reconstruction, Southern states used Jim Crow laws, poll taxes, and literacy tests to keep Black citizens apart and from voting. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) allowed separate but equal facilities, but Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ruled school segregation unconstitutional. The Civil Rights Movement used nonviolent protest and civil disobedience and won the Civil Rights Act (1964) and the Voting Rights Act (1965). Separately, the women's suffrage movement, begun at Seneca Falls in 1848, won the vote with the 19th Amendment in 1920.

concepts.definition: 13th (1865) ended slavery. 14th (1868) citizenship and equal protection. 15th (1870) no race-based voting limits.
Laws and practices, such as segregation, poll taxes, and literacy tests, that kept Black Americans apart and from voting.
concepts.tip: Jim Crow undercut the 14th and 15th Amendments.

concepts.definition: Plessy (1896) allowed separate but equal. Brown (1954) ruled separate schools unconstitutional.
Openly and peacefully breaking an unjust law and accepting the penalty.
Barred denying the vote because of sex, giving women the vote nationwide.

points: Gettysburg Address: "four score and seven years ago" points back to 1776.
Montgomery bus boycott, March on Washington, and the Voting Rights Act belong to the Civil Rights Movement.
Sectionalism over slavery helped cause the Civil War.

summary: This chapter covers America's role in the world from World War I through the Cold War.

After World War I, the Senate refused to approve the Treaty of Versailles, and the U.S. never joined the League of Nations, a sign of isolationism. The U.S. entered World War II after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941 and fought with the Allies against the Axis Powers of Germany, Italy, and Japan. At home, about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry were forced into camps.

After the war, the United States and the Soviet Union became rivals in the Cold War. The Truman Doctrine (1947) set a policy of containment, the Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe, and NATO joined the U.S. and Western Europe in a military alliance. The Cold War ended when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

concepts.definition: A policy of staying out of world affairs and foreign conflicts.
concepts.tip: Rejecting the League of Nations = isolationism.

concepts.definition: Axis: Germany, Italy, Japan. Allies: U.S., Britain, Soviet Union, China, and others.
concepts.tip: WWI Central Powers are a different group.

concepts.definition: The forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them citizens, to camps during WWII.
The Cold War policy of stopping the spread of communism, begun with the Truman Doctrine (1947).
U.S. economic aid to rebuild Western Europe after World War II.
concepts.tip: Aid, not a military alliance (that was NATO).

points: Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941) brought the U.S. into World War II.
Cold War: U.S. vs. Soviet Union, about 1947-1991.
NATO is a military alliance; the Marshall Plan was economic aid.

summary: This chapter covers the basic ideas economists use to explain choices, businesses, and trade.

Every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the next best option you give up. Incentives, such as rewards or penalties, shape choices. Entrepreneurs start businesses and take the risk, hoping to earn a profit, which is total revenue minus total costs.

Markets work best with competition; a monopoly is a single seller with no close substitutes. Specialization, where each worker or country focuses on one task, raises productivity. Countries gain by trading when each makes what it has a comparative advantage in, meaning what it gives up the least to produce.

concepts.definition: The value of the next best option you give up when you choose.
concepts.tip: Only count the best option you gave up.

concepts.definition: Total revenue minus total costs.
A market with one seller and no close substitutes.
concepts.tip: No competition often means higher prices.

concepts.definition: A reward or penalty that motivates people to act a certain way.
Focusing on one task or product, which usually raises productivity (output per worker).
Making the good you can produce at the lowest opportunity cost, then trading.
concepts.tip: Compare what each side gives up, not just who makes more.

points: Profit questions: find revenue, add all costs, then subtract.
Comparative advantage: divide to find each country's cost of one unit in terms of the other good.

summary: This chapter covers how prices are set in markets and how the whole economy is measured and managed. GED questions often show a supply and demand graph or describe a government action and ask about its effect.

Demand shows how much buyers want at each price, and supply shows how much sellers offer. Where the curves cross is the equilibrium price and quantity. If the price is above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, causing a surplus. If it is below, buyers want more than sellers offer, causing a shortage. When demand increases, the demand curve shifts right, and both the equilibrium price and quantity rise.

For the whole economy, GDP measures the value of all final goods and services produced. Inflation is a general rise in prices; deflation is a general fall. Fiscal policy is government taxing and spending, set by Congress and the President. Monetary policy is set by the Federal Reserve, which raises interest rates to slow inflation. A tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price.

concepts.definition: The price and quantity where the supply and demand curves cross.
Price above equilibrium: surplus (supply > demand). Price below: shortage (demand > supply).
concepts.tip: High price = extra goods; low price = not enough.

concepts.definition: More demand shifts the curve right; with the same supply, price and quantity both rise.
A general rise in prices over time, so each dollar buys less.
Fiscal: taxes and spending (Congress, President). Monetary: interest rates and money supply (Federal Reserve).
A tax on imported goods. It helps producers at home but raises prices for buyers.

points: On a graph, read across from the price to each line, then down to the quantity.
Surplus = quantity supplied minus quantity demanded; shortage = quantity demanded minus quantity supplied (both at that price).
Higher interest rates make borrowing cost more and slow spending.
GDP counts final goods and services produced in a country.

figures.alt: Supply line rising and demand line falling, crossing at a point marked equilibrium. A price line above equilibrium shows a gap marked surplus. A price line below equilibrium shows a gap marked shortage.
figures.caption: Above the equilibrium price there is a surplus; below it there is a shortage.

summary: This chapter covers everyday money topics: credit, saving, banking, and laws that protect borrowers.

Credit cards are revolving credit: you can borrow up to a limit, repay, and borrow again. Car loans and mortgages are installment loans with set payments. Savings accounts earn interest; simple interest equals the principal times the rate times the time.

Bank deposits at insured banks are protected by the FDIC up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each ownership category. The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to tell borrowers the APR and total finance charge before they sign.

concepts.definition: Revolving credit (credit cards) can be reused up to a limit. Installment loans (car, mortgage) are repaid in set payments.
Interest = principal x rate x time.
Protects deposits at insured banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each ownership category.
Requires lenders to disclose the APR and total finance charge.
concepts.tip: Truth = tell the true cost of credit.

points: Interest earned is not the same as the total balance.
Different consumer laws cover different things: lending costs, credit reports, and fair treatment.

summary: This chapter connects economics to major events in history.

European exploration in the 1400s and 1500s was driven by the search for trade routes to Asia and for wealth such as gold and spices. The Industrial Revolution, beginning in the 1700s, brought factories, and people moved from farms to cities for jobs.

The Great Depression began after the stock market crash of 1929. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal created programs such as Social Security (1935). During World War II, war production and military service put millions to work, and unemployment fell to very low levels.

concepts.definition: European voyages driven by trade routes to Asia, gold, spices, land, and power.
The shift to machines and factories, which drew people from farms to cities (urbanization).
FDR's programs to fight the Great Depression, including Social Security.
concepts.tip: Great Society was LBJ; Square Deal was Theodore Roosevelt.

concepts.definition: War spending and production can create jobs, as in World War II.

points: Great Depression: began after the 1929 crash.
Read data tables carefully and match the trend to the event.

summary: This chapter looks at how geography shaped early societies and how people use and change the environment.

Early civilizations, such as Egypt along the Nile and Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates, grew near rivers that gave water, rich soil, and transportation. Classical Athens developed an early direct democracy, and the Roman Republic offered a model of representative government.

People depend on natural resources. Renewable resources, such as wind and sunlight, are replaced naturally, while fossil fuels are not. Technology lets people change the environment, for example by building dams or clearing forests, with both benefits and costs. Sustainability means meeting today's needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs.

concepts.definition: Early civilizations grew along rivers for water, fertile soil, and transportation.
concepts.tip: Nile = Egypt; Tigris and Euphrates = Mesopotamia.

concepts.definition: Athens: early direct democracy. Roman Republic: elected representatives.
Renewable resources are replaced naturally (wind, sun). Nonrenewable ones take millions of years (coal, oil, gas).
Using resources so that future generations can still meet their needs.
People alter the environment by building dams, roads, and farms, or by cutting forests.
concepts.tip: Volcanoes are natural, not human changes.

points: Deforestation causes habitat loss and soil erosion.
Most human changes to the environment have both benefits and costs.

summary: This chapter covers the tools geographers use and the ways they divide the world into places and regions.

Most maps put north at the top. Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, and longitude measures distance east or west of the Prime Meridian. A map scale converts map distance to real distance, and a topographic map uses contour lines to show elevation.

A region is an area with shared features, such as climate, landforms, language, or economy. Borders can follow physical features like rivers, straight geometric lines, or cultural differences. Population density, the number of people per unit of land area, shows how crowded a place is.

concepts.definition: Latitude: north-south from the Equator. Longitude: east-west from the Prime Meridian.
concepts.tip: Latitude lines are flat like ladder rungs.

concepts.definition: Shows how map distance relates to real distance. Real distance = map distance x scale.
An area with shared physical or human features.
Physical (rivers, mountains), geometric (straight lines), cultural (language, religion).
Number of people divided by land area.
concepts.tip: 30 million / 150,000 sq mi = 200 per sq mi.

points: Contour lines close together mean steep land.
Check the zeros carefully in density and scale calculations.

summary: This chapter is about why people move and what happens to cultures when they do.

Emigration is leaving a country; immigration is moving into one. Push factors, such as war or lack of jobs, drive people away, and pull factors, such as jobs or freedom, draw them in. In the Great Migration (about 1910-1970), millions of Black Americans left the rural South for cities in the North and West, pulled by factory jobs and pushed by Jim Crow.

When cultures meet, ideas and customs spread (cultural diffusion), and newcomers often adopt the culture of their new home over generations (assimilation). A people spread far from their homeland form a diaspora. Over the past century, Americans moved steadily from rural areas to cities, a trend called urbanization.

concepts.definition: Emigration: leaving your country. Immigration: coming into a new country.
Push factors drive people away; pull factors attract them to a new place.
concepts.tip: Jim Crow pushed; factory jobs pulled.

concepts.definition: The spread of foods, ideas, music, and customs from one culture to others.
Immigrants gradually adopting the language and customs of their new country.
A people scattered from their homeland to many places.

points: The share of Americans living in urban areas roughly doubled from 1900 to 2010.
Do not mix up diffusion (customs spread) with assimilation (people adopt a culture).
